note:
The shared conformance corpus for the TSM drift contract. One input plan per
vector plus the EXPECTED output, hand-authored as intent and never read back
from an implementation. Every implementation of the contract runs this file
and compares byte-for-byte:
  - TypeScript (canonical) - 4cloudguru/terraform-drift-contract, __tests__/conformance.test.ts
  - Go driftingest         - terraform-state-manager-backend, internal/services/driftingest
  - jq                     - terraform-state-manager-backend, the dispatched CI templates
This file is byte-identical in both repositories; each side asserts the same
SHA-256 of it, so an edit to one copy reddens that repository immediately.
Fields: `expect` is the canonical summarize() Result; it states only the
NON-DEFAULT markers, and each runner fills unparseable/unmasked/truncated/
omitted_entries/omitted_attrs from the zero value. `expect_module_calls`,
when present, is the canonical moduleCallsPlan() output. `go` and `jq` record
a STATED difference for that vector - either {"rejects": why} when that
implementation refuses the document outright, or {"expect": ..., "why": ...}
when it answers differently. A difference with no entry here is a regression.
The jq expectation, when not stated, is `expect` with every attrs array
dropped: the dispatched summary is {address, actions} only and has no
attribute values at all.

vectors.why: A pure create counts once as added and carries no attrs (before is null, not an object).
An in-place update counts as changed and emits the differing top-level keys.
A pure delete counts once as destroyed; after is null so there are no attrs.
PINNED: counts are replace-aware and NOT mutually exclusive — a replacement bumps both added and destroyed, and changed stays 0 while drifted is true.
The create-before-destroy ordering counts identically; membership decides, not position.
One plan exercising every count in file order, with a skipped no-op and a skipped read interleaved.
PINNED: exactly ["no-op"] is skipped entirely — no counts and no summary row.

PINNED and the vector for contract issue #20: exactly ["read"] is skipped. The dispatched jq summarizer used to keep this row, so the same refresh-only plan produced one row from a dispatched run and none from the Action.
The skip is on the EXACT list, not on membership: ["no-op","create"] is kept and counted.
Same for ["read","create"]: kept and counted.

The vector for contract issue #21. `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` returns 2 for this plan because the output changed, but no resource changed — so `drifted` is FALSE. The dispatched jq used to take drifted from that exit code and posted true for the identical plan.
Issues #20 and #21 together: a refresh-only plan whose only changes are data-source reads plus an output. Every implementation must report zero counts, drifted false and an empty summary.
A genuinely clean plan. Note that a malformed document produces this same Result — see shape/resource-changes-not-array and contract issue #31 finding 43.
PINNED: an absent key on one side canonicalises to null, so a removed attribute reports before/after rather than being dropped.
PINNED, the other half: an explicit null and an absent key are EQUAL, so no phantom {before:null, after:null} row is emitted and the entry carries no attrs at all.

The literal key `__proto__` must be read as an own property. A bare o[k] yields Object.prototype, which serialises as {} and made a removed __proto__ attribute compare equal to an empty object and vanish.
attrs are emitted only when before AND after are both JSON objects.
PINNED: values are capped at 300 code points with a U+2026 marker.

The cap counts CODE POINTS, not UTF-16 units: 155 astral characters are 310 units but 155 code points, so nothing is truncated. This is the boundary the TypeScript fast path (length <= 300) and the Go rune count must agree on.

The shape from the Brunswick fleet drift run of 2026-10-21 (azurerm). terraform-plugin-sdk keeps `timeouts` out of the attribute diff and copies the configured value into the planned state, so a state can carry the unconfigured block as an object of nulls while the plan's after is null. Neither side carries a value and terraform plans no change for it, so `timeouts` is not reported; the resource's real change still is.
When `timeouts` is the only difference the entry carries no attrs, but the row and the counts still come from the actions. Ignoring the shape difference never hides that terraform planned an update.

Null-equivalent means null, absent, or a NON-EMPTY object or list whose every member is itself null or null-equivalent. Both sides null-equivalent is not a change: the reverse direction (a), a list-wrapped block against an absent key (b), and two null-leaved objects of different shapes (c) all carry no value on either side.

The null-equivalence applies to `timeouts` only. On any other key the shape difference can be real: an object of nulls against null is a block that is present but empty where it was absent (a), and plan JSON writes an unknown list element as null, so a list of nulls on the after side can be values known only after apply (b; this contract does not read after_unknown).

Only a value-free shape difference is ignored. A `timeouts` block with any non-null leaf, on either side, is a change and is reported: a configured timeout removed (a), and one added where the state held an object of nulls (b). Both sides of (b) are objects, so it is reported at the member that changed.

An empty object or list has no null leaf, so it is not null-equivalent: an empty list against a populated one (a) and an empty object against null (b) still show. Plan JSON drops an unknown object member, so an empty object on the after side can be an object whose every member is known only after apply.

A replacement keeps every real change, including an attribute whose after is unknown (plan JSON drops it from after, so it reads as null), while the `timeouts` shape difference is not reported (a). A replacement whose whole after is unknown is not an in-place change and carries no attrs, as before (b).

The shape of TBD3216/APP2934, ADO build 378948 (Brunswick fleet, 2026-10-22), values replaced: a central re-tag changed COST_CENTER, one of 14 tags. The whole map is past the 300-code-point value cap, so up to v1.4.2 both sides were cut mid-JSON and the changed key was in neither prefix. A changed map is reported per changed key; the 13 unchanged ones are not rows. The value-free timeouts block is still ignored.

An added key reports before null and a removed one after null, as an added or removed top-level attribute does (a). A map emptied of every tag reports each removed key (b, the availability-set shape in build 378948): both sides are objects, so the map is expanded even though one is empty.

A member key that is a terraform identifier ([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*) is named `.key`; every other key is a quoted index `["key"]`, the key as a JSON string literal in the canonical serialized form: non-ASCII and `<`/`>`/`&` raw, U+2028/U+2029 and `"` escaped. So a name parses back to one path. Rows are in code-point order of the keys, above-BMP last.
Lists of one length are expanded by index, and only the elements that differ are rows. Nested-block lists are descended the same way: a list of one block is `[0]`.

Lists of different lengths are not expanded: an element added or removed would shift every index after it. The list is one row holding both whole values, when the elements they share are equal (a) and when one of those differs too (b): index rows over the shared prefix would hide the length change.
Only an object against an object, or an array against an array, is expanded. A block that appears (null against an object), an array against an object, and a scalar against an array are each one row.

A null member equals an absent one, exactly as for top-level keys. When that is the only difference, member by member nothing differs, so the node is one row with both whole values: at the top level (a) and one level down (b). A walked node always yields at least one row, so no difference that a whole-value comparison sees is lost.

Rows are emitted depth-first: each changed top-level key in code-point order, and under it each changed member in code-point key order or index order. U+FFFF sorts before an above-BMP key here, as it does in Go and jq; a UTF-16 code-unit sort reverses them.

Expansion stops max_attr_path_depth (16) segments below the top-level key: the node there is one row holding the rest of both values whole. Objects (a) and arrays (b) alike. This bound is also the cost bound: each expanded level serialises its members once more.

A row name is never truncated, so a node is not expanded when the name of any changed member would pass max_attr_path_code_points (300); it is one row, its values capped as usual (a). A member name of exactly 300 code points is expanded (b).
The name bound counts code points, not UTF-16 units or UTF-8 bytes: a name of 300 above-BMP-heavy code points (592 UTF-16 units) is expanded (a), and one of 301 is not (b).
max_attrs_per_entry (50) bounds ROWS, so an expanded map can reach it. 51 changed tags are 51 rows: 50 are emitted in order and the 51st is counted in omitted_attrs, marking the summary truncated.

jq.why: The dispatched summary carries no attrs, so it has no attribute rows to cap: its omitted_attrs is always 0, and its truncated reports max_entries only.

vectors.why: The max_attrs_per_entry rows are shared by every changed path in an entry, so a large expansion could take all of them: 50 changed keys in a map that sorts first hid a later attribute's change (here a container image), where v1.4.2 gave every changed attribute a row. Each top-level key leaves one row for every changed key after it, so the map shows 49 of its 50 changes, the 50th is counted in omitted_attrs, and the image change keeps its row.

jq.why: The dispatched summary carries no attrs, so it has no attribute rows to cap: its omitted_attrs is always 0, and its truncated reports max_entries only.

vectors.why: When more top-level keys changed than max_attrs_per_entry allows, the first 50 changed keys each get one row (an expanded key its first changed member) and the rest are counted in omitted_attrs, as in v1.4.2.

jq.why: The dispatched summary carries no attrs, so it has no attribute rows to cap: its omitted_attrs is always 0, and its truncated reports max_entries only.

vectors.why: A member row formats its values with the same fmt() as a top-level row: a string raw, `<`/`>`/`&` raw, a number or bool as canonical JSON, null as null, a string past 300 code points cut with U+2026, and a member whose two sides are different kinds as whole canonical JSON.

PINNED: the mask is a UNION over both mirrors. A config-derived mark applies to the planned value only, so a credential routinely arrives marked on exactly one side; masking per-side emitted the other verbatim.
The mirror image of the above.
The symmetric case, unchanged by the union.

PINNED and deliberate (contract issue #10): a plan carrying no sensitivity metadata gets NO masking. Masking here would mask every attribute of every such plan. All implementations fail open identically; see SECURITY.md.
A mark nested in an object mirror masks the key. The value is a string, so there is nothing to expand and the row is masked whole.
An EMPTY mirror container holds no truthy scalar, so it is not a mark.
An array mirror holding a mark masks the key. The value is a string, so the row is masked whole. A non-empty array with no mark in it is not one: see masking/list-of-false-is-not-a-mark.
A mirror that is not an object is the whole-value flag: true masks every key.
PINNED: a present-but-falsy mirror masks nothing. This is the same fail-open decision as masking/neither-mirror; it is recorded so it cannot change silently.
PINNED ordering: a marked value 310 code points long emits the literal "(sensitive)", NOT a 300-code-point prefix of the secret. The mask must run before the formatter, not after it.

The shape of TBD4545/APP6233, ADO builds 378968 and 379017, with the mirrors of a real azurerm 4.81.0 plan: terraform writes `blob_properties` as `[{"container_delete_retention_policy":[{}],"cors_rule":[],"delete_retention_policy":[{}],"restore_policy":[]}]`, a container for every nested block with no `true` in it. Up to v1.4.2 any non-empty container masked the key, so the retention change rendered (sensitive) -> (sensitive). A mark is a truthy scalar at some depth; this mirror has none, so the change is shown at its leaves. The account keys and connection strings, which azurerm marks `true`, are changed rotations here and stay masked.

terraform writes a list of primitives as a list of `false`s: a real azurerm 4.81.0 `address_space` of two CIDRs is `[false,false]`. Up to v1.4.2 that masked the key. It holds no truthy scalar, so it is not a mark, whether the list is expanded (a) or one row (b).

A real azurerm 4.81.0 linux_web_app mirror: `docker_registry_password` is the one sensitive leaf, three blocks deep, so only that path is masked and its changed siblings are shown (a). The union holds at every depth: marked on the after side only (b, a config-derived mark), it is masked on both sides.

azurerm marks `connection_string` as a whole block: the real 4.81.0 mirror is `true`, not a member-by-member map. A truthy scalar covers everything under it, so nothing is expanded into view, including the unmarked-looking `name`.

A sensitive variable placed in a map: terraform marks the element (`{"SECRET":true}`, real 4.81.0 shape), not the map. The marked element is masked and its unmarked sibling is shown. The key is shown, as terraform shows it.
A map marked as a whole is one masked row: expanding it would put its KEYS in row names, and a key can carry the secret.
A node that is not expanded is one row, masked when either mirror holds a mark anywhere under it: lists of different lengths (a), and a block that appears where there was none (b).

Not terraform output: a mirror whose shape is not the value's (an array mirror on an object value, an object mirror on an array value) cannot be aligned member by member. When it holds a mark it masks the whole value rather than being skipped by the walk (a, b). When it holds none it is no mark (c).

Not terraform output, which writes only `true`: a mark is any truthy scalar, by the Python truthiness the whole-value flag already uses, so a non-empty string or a non-zero number masks, at the path (a, b) or inside a mirror container (e, f). Up to v1.4.2 only `true` and a non-empty container did. A falsy scalar (`0`, `""`) is no mark (c, d).

Marks are aligned by path, and a value can change path between the two sides. A value a mirror marks anywhere in the change is masked wherever else it appears: moved to another index in a list of one length (a), under a renamed map key next to a config-derived mark on the after side only (b), and in another attribute, as a member row or inside a whole-value row (c). The union applies here too: a value is marked when EITHER mirror marks its path, so the old plaintext of an attribute that only the after side marks is masked when it turns up elsewhere (d). Path masking alone emitted the unmarked occurrence of each, where v1.4.2 masked the whole attribute.

A row name carries map keys out in the clear, so a node is not expanded when a changed member's key is a marked value; it is one row, masked because it holds that value (a). Keys under a marked map are themselves marked values, so one turning up as a value elsewhere is masked (b).

A marked empty string, boolean or null carries no secret and is everywhere, so it does not mask other rows that hold the same value (a). A marked number masks the same number elsewhere, and not the string of it (b). A value that merely contains a marked value is not masked (c): only exact values are.

Booleans, null and "" are not held as marked values (masking/marked-values-are-strings-and-numbers), so for them the path rule is the only mask, and it holds at every depth: a marked flag inside a nested block (a), one marked on the after side only (b, the union), and one inside a value that is not expanded, marked on the after side only (c).
A mark below the depth bound is not lost: the node at the bound is one row, and it is masked because a mark sits under it.
Non-ASCII is emitted raw, never \uXXXX-escaped. (The retracted json.dumps claim would have escaped it.)
Same for object keys.

Contract issue #17: keys sort by CODE POINT. U+FFFF sorts BEFORE U+1F600. JavaScript’s default comparator sorts by UTF-16 code unit and put the emoji first, disagreeing with the Go mirror (UTF-8 byte order) and with jq for a key set an attacker can choose.

Contract issue #17: U+2028 and U+2029 are escaped inside a serialised value. Go’s encoding/json escapes them unconditionally with no flag to disable it, so this is the side that moved; it is also the safer form, since a raw U+2028 terminates a line in a JS context.

Contract issue #17: `<`, `>` and `&` are emitted raw. Go’s encoding/json HTML-escapes them by DEFAULT, so the mirror must serialise through an encoder with SetEscapeHTML(false). These three characters appear in every IAM policy document and user_data script, making this the highest-frequency divergence of the set.
Uppercase sorts before lowercase: code points, not a locale collation.
Contract issue #18: negative zero serialises as -0. JSON.stringify(-0) yields "0", which lost the sign Terraform reported and disagreed with the Go mirror.
2.0 and 2 are the same double and serialise identically in both implementations.

A top-level string attribute value is NOT serialised — it passes through as-is, so `<` and even a raw U+2028 reach the summary unescaped. Both implementations do this; only NESTED strings go through the serializer.
Contract issue #17, on the OTHER key set: the attrs array itself is ordered by the union of before/after keys, and that sort must be code-point too.
Contract issue #18: because -0 serialises as -0, a 0 -> -0 change is reported. Before the fix TypeScript rendered both as "0" and dropped the attribute while the Go mirror reported it.

PINNED and NOT a divergence: JSON parsing maps every number to an IEEE-754 double in BOTH implementations, so two distinct 20-digit serials become the same value and the attribute is dropped. Contract issue #18 reported this as a TypeScript-vs-reference divergence; it is not one — the implementations agree, and changing it is a parse-boundary decision in every consumer, not an edit inside summarize(). This vector exists so that agreement is asserted rather than assumed. The two serials here are textually DISTINCT in this file and must stay that way: each runner's own parse is what collapses them, which is the behaviour under test. An earlier revision stored both sides as 12345678901234567000 -- the already-collapsed value, produced by round-tripping the authored literals through a JSON writer -- so the vector asserted only that an update with no attribute change emits no attrs, and would have passed just as happily if the collapse were fixed.
true and 1 are different canonical forms, so the change is reported.

Equality compares CANONICAL forms ("1" vs 1), so this is a change — even though both sides RENDER as the identical string "1", because a top-level string passes through unquoted. The rendered attr looking unchanged is expected, not a bug.
Contract issue #15 residual: two entries with no address both key on "". Real plans always populate address; this is recorded, not fixed, because the address is the summary’s primary key.
PINNED (contract issue #15): the address is deliberately NOT capped, because it is how a drift record is matched to a resource. It IS type-checked. See SECURITY.md.
Contract issue #15: a non-string address is emitted as "" rather than put into a field the exported type declares string.

go.rejects: driftingest types address as string, so json.Unmarshal fails and /drift/ingest answers 422 for the whole document. Fail-closed, and a different answer from the contract’s.

jq.why: The dispatched jq copies .address through with no type check, so the stored row carries an object in a string field.

vectors.why: Contract issue #31 finding 43: a malformed document reports drifted:false, identical to a genuinely clean plan. Recorded here so the three answers to the same garbage are written down.

go.rejects: json.Unmarshal fails on the string, so /drift/ingest answers 422 — the only implementation that tells the operator anything.

vectors.why: A wrong-typed actions list degrades to an uncounted-but-PRESENT row rather than a silently dropped one, and never puts a non-array into a field SummaryEntry declares string[].

go.rejects: json.Unmarshal fails on the string actions; /drift/ingest answers 422.

jq.why: The dispatched jq copies .change.actions through with no type check.

vectors.why: Terraform always writes actions, so this reaches only a hand-built plan — but the three implementations answer differently and that difference is a real shape difference for a consumer that iterates the array.

go.why: Go marshals its nil []string as null where the contract emits [].

jq.why: jq copies the absent field through as null, like Go.

vectors.why: A JSON null inside resource_changes is valid JSON. The contract skips it; the dispatched jq used to emit a {address:null, actions:null} row for it, which is the same row-set divergence as issue #20 in the same expression, so it was fixed in the same change.

go.why: A JSON null unmarshals into a zero-valued ResourceChange, which is not skipped, so Go emits a leading empty row.

vectors.why: Contract issue #31 finding 43. An empty object parses fine and used to produce the IDENTICAL Result as a verified-clean plan — added 0, drifted false, empty summary. A `terraform show -json` document always carries resource_changes, so its absence means this is not a plan: a truncated show, the wrong file handed to the callback, or a broken pipeline step. Now says so.
An explicit null is the same non-answer as an absent key.

Contract issue #11. A 60-level nested value serialises past the 300-code-point cap and both implementations must truncate the same prefix. The crash this issue reported is TypeScript-only and unbounded (the recursive serializer threw RangeError around 2,600 levels, out of summarize() and into the consumer CI step, suppressing the drift report); the serializer is now iterative and cannot throw at any depth, which no shared vector can express because Go rejects anything past encoding/json own 10,000 nesting cap at the unmarshal boundary. This vector pins the part they CAN both answer.

The plan’s configuration block carries no sensitivity metadata at all, so it is projected to the two fields the backend reads, with source credentials scrubbed. expressions, the recursive module subtree and every other member are dropped by construction.

go.rejects: driftingest.Plan types module_calls as a map of structs, so the `notobj` entry (an array) fails json.Unmarshal and /drift/ingest answers 422 for the WHOLE document — discarding an otherwise valid summary. Fail-closed, pre-existing, and an availability difference rather than a disclosure; the contract coerces to {} and summarizes normally. Go does not implement moduleCallsPlan() at all — it only reads source/version_constraint into driftingest.Configuration — so the provenance projection below is asserted against the jq mirror.

vectors.why: Contract issue #17 on the module-name key set: jq’s `keys` sorts by code point, so the TypeScript sort had to move to match the dispatched payload for the identical plan.
Every emitted provenance string goes through the same 300-code-point cap as an attribute value.

resource_drift is processed independently of resource_changes: a plan with no unapplied changes but one hand-edited resource reports zero added/changed/destroyed and a non-zero drift_added, with drift_summary carrying the row summary omits.

resource_changes and resource_drift are counted and summarised on independent tracks: an unapplied update does not touch drift_added/drift_summary, and a drifted create/delete pair does not touch added/changed/destroyed/summary.

PINNED: resource_drift honours the identical skip rule as resource_changes -- exactly ["no-op"] or ["read"] entries are skipped from both drift counts and drift_summary. The plan is explicit that drift counting reuses these rules rather than a parallel copy; a divergence between the two paths is the bug this phase exists to avoid.
resource_drift is optional and purely additive: a plan that omits it entirely reports zero drift counts and an empty drift_summary, and existing resource_changes handling is unaffected.

resource_drift attrs are bounded by the same max_attrs_per_entry as resource_changes: 51 differing top-level keys on one drifted resource emit only the first 50 in code-point order, the 51st silently dropped by the shared cap.
resource_drift attrs go through the identical masking rule as resource_changes: a key marked sensitive on either mirror renders "(sensitive)" in drift_summary rather than the raw value.
`resource_drift` runs through the identical walk: a hand-edited tag is reported per key and a marked leaf is masked, in drift_summary.

The realistic shape of masking/marked-value-at-another-path: terraform's refresh re-applies the prior marks to the refreshed value by path, so after an out-of-band reorder the mark stays on index 0 on both sides and the secret sits unmarked at index 1 of the after value. It is masked there because it is marked elsewhere in the change.
